extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato; philosophers, literary theorists, and creative writers interested in the ethics and epistemology of imitation
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Plato (Republic Books IX–X) arguing that imitative poetry is thrice removed from truth and can mislead the soul; evaluates poets by their knowledge, moral effect, and closeness to reality. Relevant for assessing the ethical and epistemic value of literary imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative poetry is ruinous to the understanding of the hearers
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘All poetical imitations are ruinous to the understanding of the hearers… the knowledge of their true nature is the only antidote to them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato argues that poetry (imitative art) addresses appearances rather than truth and so misleads the audience. As guidance, treat imitative works cautiously: they can inculcate false images and passions unless corrected by knowledge. Example/anti-pattern: allowing tragic poets unlimited influence because their rhetoric deceives the ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic distance from truth (thrice removed)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The imitator… is thrice removed from the king and from the truth’ (three levels of creators: the Form/Divine maker, the craftsman/maker, and the painter/imitator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by how closely they approach the Form/true reality rather than mere appearance. Imitative art occupies the furthest remove and so carries the weakest claim to truth. Scoring note: closer fidelity to underlying truth or knowledge earns higher epistemic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets/imitators lack true knowledge of their subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitator knows appearances only and not the true nature or function of the things he portrays; e.g., Homer is shown not to have been a legislator or practical teacher of the arts he sings about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge authors on whether they possess demonstrable knowledge of the subject matter they represent. Anti-pattern: poets who use persuasive form (rhythm, melody) to mask ignorance. Example guidance: a work claiming political or ethical insight should be backed by genuine understanding, not just ornamental language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry appeals to inferior parts of the soul and can be morally harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation addresses the parts of the soul that are irrational or deceptive and so may foment passions, confusion, or vice rather than reason and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literature by its psychological and moral effects: does it rouse baser impulses or cultivate reason and harmony? Works that systematically excite the irrational parts of readers are treated as harmful; desirable works should support the rational/calculating principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (melody/rhythm) can conceal lack of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody, rhythm, and harmony give a ‘sweet influence’ that can make ignorant listeners think a poet knows many arts; stripped of musical form, poetic tales appear poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should separate formal attractiveness from substantive truth: ornate style should not automatically count as knowledge or moral worth. Anti-pattern: valuing a piece primarily for its musical or rhetorical charm when it lacks truthful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate literature by whether it makes men better or worse
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems and poets should be judged by whether they educate and improve private and public life; the standard asked of Homer is whether any city was made better by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social/educational impact as an evaluative criterion: works that inculcate virtue, civic harmony, or wisdom are valued; works that corrupt character or mislead civic judgment are disqualified. Example scoring: pedagogical/legislative benefit counts highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for realities over appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation imitates appearance, not the reality; painters and poets represent how things seem, not how they truly are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer creative work that reveals or engages with deeper realities (forms, truths) rather than merely reproducing surface appearances. Anti-pattern: writing that traffics only in deceptive or shifting appearances without anchoring in any stable insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: The excellence of a work is relative to its use and the user's knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The excellence or beauty or truth of every structure… is relative to the use for which nature or the artist has intended them… the user of them must have the greatest experience.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fictional or artistic artifacts for functional correctness relative to their aims and intended users. For example, depictions of technical practices should reflect the perspective of practitioners; the user/reader's needs and expertise matter when judging success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is play/sport and tends to pander to popular opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is likened to play; imitators will imitate what appears good to the ignorant multitude rather than what is truly good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware works that prioritize popular appeal over truth or moral seriousness. Criterion: distinguish art that challenges and elevates public taste from art that merely panders for applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts that cultivate reason (measuring, numbering, weighing) are preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato praises arts of measure, calculation and weight as allied to the calculating and rational principle in the soul and as remedies for illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value aspects of creative work that encourage measurement, clarity, logical structure, and rational reflection. In practice, give credit to works that stimulate critical thinking and resist purely illusory persuasion.
